q.q: You open a $1,000 long at 10x. How much margin did you put up, and how large is the position?
o: $1,000 margin, $10,000 position
$100 margin, $1,000 position
$1,000 margin, $1,000 position
$100 margin, $10,000 position
q.w: In futures the size of a trade is the position. Margin is the position divided by leverage: $1,000 / 10 = $100.

q.q: BTC is at $60,000. You go long at 20x with a 0.5% maintenance margin. Ignoring fees, about where are you liquidated?
q.w: Long liquidation = entry x (1 - 1/leverage + maintenance) = 60,000 x (1 - 0.05 + 0.005) = $57,300.

q.q: Two traders risk the same dollar amount with the same stop price. One uses 5x and the other uses 25x with a smaller margin. What changes?
o: The 25x trader can lose more dollars if the stop fills
Nothing about the loss at the stop, but the 25x liquidation sits closer to entry
The 25x trader pays lower fees
The 5x trader makes less if the trade wins
q.w: Same position size and same stop means the same loss at the stop. Higher leverage only means less margin and a liquidation price closer to entry.

q.q: Your account is $2,000 and you risk 1% per trade. Your stop is 2% from entry. What position size fits?
q.w: Risk is 1% of $2,000 = $20. Position = risk / stop distance = $20 / 0.02 = $1,000.

q.q: A trade risks $50 to make $75. You win 35% of the time. Ignoring fees, what happens over many trades?
o: You lose about $6 a trade on average
You make about $4 a trade on average
You break even
You make about $26 a trade on average
q.w: 0.35 x $75 - 0.65 x $50 = $26.25 - $32.50 = about -$6.25. A good-looking ratio is not enough without the win rate to match.

q.q: After losing 20% of an account, what gain do you need just to get back to where you started?
q.w: $100 down 20% is $80, and $20 on $80 is 25%. Losses need bigger gains to repair, which is why position size matters more than entries.

q.q: You open and close a $10,000 position. The taker fee is 0.055% per side. What do the fees cost in total?
q.w: Fees are charged on the position, on both sides: $10,000 x 0.055% x 2 = $11, whatever margin you used.

q.q: Funding is positive on a perpetual. You hold a short through the funding time. What happens?
o: You pay funding to the longs
Nobody pays while the price is rising
The exchange takes it as a fee from both sides
You receive funding from the longs
q.w: Positive funding means longs pay shorts. It moves between traders, and the exchange does not keep it.

q.q: You set a stop-market order at $95 on a long, and price gaps from $97 to $93. Where do you most likely get filled?
o: Exactly $95
At your entry price
Near $93, worse than your stop
The stop is cancelled by the gap
q.w: A stop-market order becomes a market order once triggered, so it fills at the next available price. A stop limits the plan, not the worst case.

q.q: A coin drops 8% in an hour and open interest falls sharply at the same time. What is the likeliest reading?
o: New shorts are piling in
Long positions are being closed or liquidated
Spot buyers are taking over
Funding has turned off
q.w: Falling price with falling open interest means positions are leaving the market. New shorts would raise open interest.

q.q: Price has made higher highs and higher lows for a week. It now breaks below the last higher low on heavy volume. What changed?
o: The trend is confirmed
Nothing, a single candle never matters
The structure of the uptrend is broken
It is a guaranteed reversal
q.w: An uptrend is defined by higher lows, so losing one breaks the structure. That is information, not a guarantee of a reversal.

q.q: A level has held four times. Price is back at it, moving fast, on rising funding. A clean breakout candle closes just above resistance. What should worry you most?
o: A close back below the level soon after, which traps late buyers
That four touches make a level stronger for ever
That a break above resistance is impossible
That funding only matters for shorts
q.w: Failed breakouts are common. A close back under the level leaves late buyers trapped, and their stops become fuel for the drop.

q.q: You lost three trades in a row, all inside your plan. You feel you must win it back today. What is the right move?
o: Double the size on the next trade
Move your stops further away
Switch to a coin that is moving more
Take your normal size or stop for the day, as your rules say
q.w: Three planned losses are normal. Raising size to win it back is revenge trading, which turns a normal streak into a real drawdown.

q.q: A trade is near your stop. You are sure it will turn around. What do you do?
o: Leave the stop where it is
Move the stop further away to give it room
Remove the stop and watch closely
Add to the position at a better price
q.w: A stop is decided before the trade, when you can think clearly. Moving it is letting the fear of a loss make the decision.

q.q: You made 40% in a month on paper by breaking your rules three times. What is the honest conclusion?
o: Your rules are too strict and should go
You are ready for bigger size
Part of that result is luck you cannot repeat
Paper results always carry over to live trading
q.w: A result earned by breaking your rules says little about your process. Judge the process, not one month's number.

bands.p: Nothing to be ashamed of: this is what the test is for. Trading futures with these gaps is how accounts get wiped. Learn the basics first, free, and practise with paper money.

faq: How does the Trader Readiness Test work?

It is 15 questions on leverage, risk, costs, reading the market and discipline. You get your score at once, a result for each area, and the reasoning behind every answer. It takes about five minutes, is free, and needs no account.
Does a high score mean I should trade real money?
No. The test measures knowledge. It cannot measure how you behave when a trade goes against you, and nothing here is financial advice. Futures trading can lose your whole stake.
Yes, as often as you like. The questions do not change, so the second score says less than the first. The Academy has full lessons and harder final exams for each topic.
